messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Questions regarding initial values for (pre-)warmup
parts:
These questions are mostly for Micheal. I've asked before, but it got buried in other discussion.

In src/stan/gm/command.hpp, when a sampler is called and we start warmup, under most samplers we call:
   init_adapt<sampler>(sampler_ptr, adapt)  (lines 835-875)

This calls:
   s->init_stepsize() (line 231)

When we start init_stepsize(), the sampler's position elements are always initialized with 0.


**** Questions ***
Is this the intended behavior?
Should we be adapting an initial stepsize starting from the initialization? (we've already drawn the initial values or loaded the file by this point)
Or should we be starting from a different starting point?
Or... does it not matter, which is why it's starting at 0?



Daniel

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Questions regarding initial values for (pre-)warmup
parts: > Is this the intended behavior?
I'm not sure what the true indented behavior is supposed to be, namely I can't remember what part of the code is historical and what part was intentional.

> Should we be adapting an initial stepsize starting from the initialization? (we've already drawn the initial values or loaded the file by this point)
> Or should we be starting from a different starting point?
> Or... does it not matter, which is why it's starting at 0?
Because it's just trying to find a decent starting value it probably doesn't matter that much, but it's more consistent if we initialize the position of the sampler first.

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Questions regarding initial values for (pre-)warmup
parts: On Fri, Dec 6, 2013 at 3:34 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Is this the intended behavior?

I'm not sure what the true indented behavior is supposed to be, namely I can't remember what part of the code is historical and what part was intentional.
Ok. Just so it's clear, since it always starts at 0, even if we can't evaluate log_prob() at that point, it'll try to start adaptation from there. Always.

> Should we be adapting an initial stepsize starting from the initialization? (we've already drawn the initial values or loaded the file by this point)
> Or should we be starting from a different starting point?
> Or... does it not matter, which is why it's starting at 0?

Because it's just trying to find a decent starting value it probably doesn't matter that much, but it's more consistent if we initialize the position of the sampler first.

Should we:
1. grab the initial point through one of these options:
  - random initialization
  - init file
2. create the sampler
3. *** initialize with the initial point.
4. find starting values.
5. Before sampling, reinitialize the sampler with the initial point.
6. sample.
??

We currently have a different #3:
3. no initialization of initial point. (this is implicitly all 0).

I didn't understand what Daniel said the current code's
doing, but my understanding of what it should do is this:

1. take user-specified inits theta0

(user will specify a random range [explicitly or by default]
or give us actual initial values)

2. find an initial step size epsilon based on theta0

3. start warmup iterations from theta0 with initial step size epsilon

I don't know if things got broken on the current develop
branch, but I'm not seeing my user-specified inits just being
ignored in 2.0.1. On the other hand, we did get a message from a user
reporting exactly that, so I'm not sure what's going on.

Daniel --- I think it's worth delaying 2.1 to validate that
this works on our de facto corpus of models (the content of
which is just the fastest of the BUGS models plus the funnel
at the moment).

Also, how much of this code's duplicated in RStan and PyStan? We
want all of our implementations to match when given the same
specs and same seed.

- Bob

parts: Thanks for clarifying!
On Fri, Dec 13, 2013 at 2:19 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

I didn't understand what Daniel said the current code's
doing, but my understanding of what it should do is this:

  1.  take user-specified inits theta0

      (user will specify a random range [explicitly or by default]
       or give us actual initial values)

  2.  find an initial step size epsilon based on theta0

  3.  start warmup iterations from theta0 with initial step size epsilon
It is currently not doing this. It is doing this:

1. take user-specified inits theta0    

      (user will specify a random range [explicitly or by default]
       or give us actual initial values)

(if random, try to initialize up to MAX_INIT_TRIES=100 times)

2. find an initial step size epsilon based on 0 (not theta0)
3. start warmup iterations from theta0 with initial step size epsilon

The difference is Step 2. I can imagine a situation where a random initialization is fine, but trying to find an initial step size epsilon starting at 0 can fail. I just haven't been clever enough to create an example of this.

I don't know if things got broken on the current develop
branch, but I'm not seeing my user-specified inits just being
ignored in 2.0.1.  On the other hand, we did get a message from a user
reporting exactly that, so I'm not sure what's going on.

Yes, that's the right behavior. The user-specified inits are being used. If you remember from the user model, the user was using variance(). Randomly generated parameters would result in a non-NaN gradients whereas init=0 would. That's how I stumbled on our current behavior.

Daniel --- I think it's worth delaying 2.1 to validate that
this works on our de facto corpus of models (the content of
which is just the fastest of the BUGS models plus the funnel
at the moment).
Ok. Just FYI, our code currently runs on BUGS, but learns initial step size epsilon based on 0, not based on theta0.

Also, how much of this code's duplicated in RStan and PyStan?  We
want all of our implementations to match when given the same
specs and same seed.

The initialization would have to change in command.hpp, so I'm assuming we'd have to push across the board to all our interfaces.

Thanks again for clarifying.
